kicker: Chapter 15 · Direction is the scarce skill
title: How cheap is it to undo?
subtitle: Not "do I trust the agent", which has no answer, but: if this is wrong, how cheap is it to undo, and what does it break before I do?
alt: A decision tree. The question in the middle: if this is wrong, how cheap is it to undo, and what does it break before I do? To the left, the two-way door: an article, where a correction is a new version, or a narrow internal tool that can be switched off; there, use controls that do not get tired: a validator, a policy row enforced outside the model, a record read afterwards. To the right, the one-way door: an email in my name, or a tool that touches regulated data every day; there, put the person: sending in my name, typing a secret, spending money, deleting what has no backup.

checked: Not "do I trust the agent", which has no answer, but: if this is wrong, how cheap is it to undo, and what does it break before I do?
An article is a two-way door: a correction is a new version, and the next reader gets the fixed page. An email in my name is a one-way door.
A narrow internal tool that a few people use and that can be switched off is a two-way door
A tool that touches regulated data every day is a one-way door
use controls that do not get tired: a validator, a policy row enforced outside the model, a record read afterwards.
sending in my name, typing a secret, spending money, deleting what has no backup
footnote: Why not a person everywhere: people approve almost everything they are shown; Anthropic measured that its coding agent's users approve 93% of permission prompts.
source_line: Source: chapter 15, Direction is the scarce skill (v2.0.0-rc2), from the newsroom's How cheap is it to undo, and Jeff Bezos's 2015 letter on one-way and two-way doors. The 93% is Anthropic's measurement, as the chapter cites it.
